overview: Sabini is the Latin name behind the English “Sabines”, communities of ancient central Italy. This shared card focuses on evidence from Cures and Eretum in the Tiber valley. The map splits the name between 500 to 323 BCE and 323 to 300 BCE; its broad, changing outlines are not verified Sabine borders. Earlier finds below provide context, and neither cutoff marks the disappearance of these communities.

periods.title: Houses, workshops and rich burials
periods.summary: Earlier evidence from Cures and Eretum reveals households and powerful families. These are broad archaeological phases, not the dates of one unified kingdom.

periods.title: Changing settlements and Roman expansion
periods.summary: Cemetery use at Colle del Forno changed over time, including renewed burial in the fourth and early third centuries BCE.

sections.title: A house with a loom and an oven

items.text: At Cures, archaeologists reconstructed an eighth-century BCE hut with two rooms. A rectangular room held a loom and other domestic activities; a rounded room contained an oven and cooking and serving pots. Making clothes and preparing meals shared a very compact address.

The settlement also had water cisterns, grain stores and a clay-settling tank connected to a pottery kiln. Water storage and food reserves were practical necessities. The evidence describes those installations; it does not identify a toilet system or tell us how every household disposed of waste.

Local pottery stood alongside imported Etruscan vessels. Bronze ornaments, pins and beads of glass paste and amber also survive. These objects show craft skills and connections with neighbouring communities; they do not mean everyone could afford the same wardrobe or tableware.

Archaeologist Alessandro Guidi describes a Cures hut apparently abandoned after a fire, probably beginning in the oven room. Burned deposits preserved dozens of complete or reconstructible pots. A terrible day for its occupants left an unusually useful record of what had been inside.

Several fine vessels occurred in pairs or sets of four or six. Guidi connects their decoration, fabric and repeated forms with shared meals or banquets. That is an interpretation of this particular collection, not proof that every Sabine dinner came with matching crockery.

An early sixth-century BCE burial at Eretum contained a carriage decorated with bronze, elaborate horse equipment and expensive vessels. Spits and fire supports suggest the ritual importance of banqueting. A rich funeral displays what a powerful group wanted remembered, not an average family’s grocery list.

After the middle of that century, monumental family tombs reveal another way of displaying authority. Some male burials included a lituus, a curved staff associated with an augur’s religious office. Political influence and religious responsibilities could belong to the same powerful families.

A later sixth-century tomb contained a terracotta throne and evidence of sacrificed horses. The CNR report interprets its occupant as a king. The objects support an argument about exceptional rank; they do not supply a complete list of rulers or the borders of their power.

sections.title: A small sample of surviving writing

items.text: “toútaíh” is a scholarly transliteration of a word on the Cures stone inscription. Linguist Raoul Zamponi glosses its noun as “people, community” and identifies the form as locative singular. It belongs to the South Picene inscription corpus; this is a real ancient word, presented in modern Latin-letter transcription.

The stone has two lines running from right to left. Its line break is a distinctive feature within the group discussed by the museum. We can study a writer’s choices even when much of the message remains difficult to interpret; surviving inscriptions cannot tell us how many children learned to write.

sections.title: Family memory and modern detective work

items.text: Colle del Forno’s underground chamber tombs had wall recesses and access corridors. Older and newer burials occupied the same tombs, showing repeated use over generations. Those spaces preserve evidence of continued burial traditions, though they cannot give us a complete family tree.

Tomb 11 was robbed in 1970. At least 145 objects were sold to a Copenhagen museum the following year and returned to Italy in 2016. Recovering them helped bring a scattered archaeological story back together. Knowing where an object came from matters as much as admiring its shine.

ending.text: Roman expansion brought the region under Roman power; the Fara in Sabina museum identifies the campaign of Manius Curius Dentatus in 290 BCE as the turning point. This falls after both imported map cutoffs. A change of rulers did not make the inhabitants vanish, and the archaeological record should not be compressed into the ending of one uniform Sabine state.
